verdicts.note: Attacked on strength: the hospital's FAQ hopes the modernization lets it end the annual $1.46 million ER operating levy (S5), which would offset part of the new tax. But the dossier records that as 'an expectation, not a commitment in the ballot title' (S1, S5), and the measure replaces no existing bond levy (S1, S5). A yes vote adds a new excess property tax of about $0.73 per $1,000 (S1; $219 a year on $300,000, S4) for up to 30 years on up to $48 million of bonds (S1). That is a brand-new levy, which the Grant and King scales put at 2. S1, S4 and S5 exist in the dossier and support the basis. Spending was considered and not proposed: the bonds remodel and re-equip the existing hospital (S1, S3); 'expand diagnostics' (S3) is one item in a modernization list, and the opposing case is about how, not whether, to spend on care (S1). No local-control mapping: Sorensen's call for a county-wide study (S1) is about planning, not state or regional authority.

what_it_does matches S1, S2, S7 and S8 ($48 million, up to 30 years, 'construct, equip, remodel, renovate'; 'from Mansfield to Mazama'; the $45 million 2025 bond at 52.3%; 60% needed). cost_line matches S1 ($0.73, $18 a month) and S4 ($219 a year). pro_summary matches S1 and S3 (Pruett as board chair; 'keep quality healthcare close to home'; community-owned; 'practical investment' in patient spaces, technology and infrastructure; wildfire and emergency resilience). con_summary has two statements the dossier does not support. (1) 'compete for patients and staff': the rebuttal says the three hospitals 'have few overnight patients and compete with each other' (S1); staff is not mentioned. (2) 'the bond funds construction, not operations': no such argument from Sorensen appears in the dossier. It also attributes everything to 'the statement against', but the competition, 'fragile' and Medicaid points come from his rebuttal (S1), and it leaves out his central claim that $48 million and 30 years of taxes 'locks in the current system' and that a study might favor a central facility with outlying urgent care. Suggested con_summary: "The statement against (Melvin Sorensen) says voters should first get solid county-wide information on how best to meet Okanogan County's medical needs, and that committing $48 million and 30 years of taxes locks in the current system; a study might favor a central hospital with outlying 24-hour urgent care. His rebuttal says the county's three small hospitals have few overnight patients and compete with each other, that Three Rivers is fragile, and that if it failed residents would face decades of taxes with no hospital."

Attacked from both sides. Toward 2: it is a property tax above regular limits (S10). Toward 0: it changes nothing from today. Neither holds. It is the same $80,000 at about $0.36 per $1,000 as the 2025 and 2026 collections (S1, S4, S5), on a levy voters have renewed every cycle the dossier checked (S6-S9). A same-amount renewal maps to 1 on the King/Spokane/Grant scale (Rockford, Spangle, Wilson Creek). A yes vote still continues a tax a no vote would end, so 0 is wrong. S1, S4 and S5 support the basis. No spending axis: it pays for routine operation of the existing ambulance and clinic (S1).

what_it_does matches S1 and S3 (one-year levy; ambulance service and a clinic contracted with Wenatchee Valley Medical Center; 'Waterville Ambulance' letterhead) and S6-S9 (approved 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025). 'Asks for the same levy every year' is a fair reading of the dossier's table, though amounts before 2025 were not retrieved; nothing contradicts it. cost_line matches S1, S4 and S5, and $108 on $300,000 is correct arithmetic. pro_summary correctly says no statement was filed and paraphrases the explanatory statement ('sufficient funds', S1). con_summary matches S1.

Hardest attack: the dossier notes that for the 2024 bond the district promised 'no change to the combined tax rate of $2.92' (S4). If the 2026 bond also keeps the combined rate level, a yes vote would mostly continue an existing school tax burden, which might argue for 1. But the 2026 page does not say so (S3), the dossier refuses to assume it, and the measure is a new $125 million authorization, not a renewal (S1), following three failed attempts (S8-S10). On the record, a yes vote authorizes a new excess levy of about $0.79 per $1,000 for 20 years (S1, S3), which King and Grant map at 2 for new bond levies. S1 and S3 support the basis. Spending was considered and not proposed: the bond rebuilds the oldest wings of three existing elementaries and replaces 15 portables with permanent classrooms (S1, S3). That converts temporary space rather than adding schools, unlike the Auburn fifth-middle-school precedent, and no opposition argues about scale. parental-rights is correctly left unmapped: the measure is about buildings, not curricula, notification or opt-outs (S1).

what_it_does matches S1 and S3 ($125 million; 20 years; Kenroy 1958, Lee 1957, Cascade 1967; 15 portables; security entrances, roofs, HVAC, parking, tennis courts and bleachers elsewhere; about $25 million in state aid) and S8-S10 (failed 2022 at 51.26%; 2024 at 59.56% and 59.04%). cost_line matches S3 ($0.79, $32.92 a month, $395 a year on $500,000) and correctly reports that the page does not say whether the rate is on top of the current one (S3, S4). pro_summary matches the statement for in S1 (committee names; 'aging, overcrowded, and increasingly expensive to maintain'; 15 portables; 162 exterior doors; pickup away from busy streets; about $25 million in state assistance). con_summary matches S1.

Attacked toward 2: the area pays no fire-district tax today (S5, S6), and once formed the board may impose a regular levy up to $0.50 per $1,000 without another vote (S9), with more under RCW 52.16.140 and 52.16.160 (S10, S11). That makes a yes vote the gateway to a brand-new tax, which the Grant scale would put at 2. Attacked toward 0: the proposition itself sets no levy (S1, S2). The scorer's 1 is the right middle: a yes vote clearly aligns with a new tax, since the ballot says the district would be 'financed by a property tax levy' (S1), but neither the rate nor a budget is set or known (no district budget or planned rate was found). S1, S6, S9, S10 and S11 all exist in the dossier; S6 supports the claim that no district covers the area today. The dossier's reason for not mapping local-control is sound under the issue #19 addendum: forming a local special district is not about state mandates or regional authorities.

what_it_does matches S1-S3 and S5-S8 (about 29.1 square miles; Ephrata postal addresses; fire district code 000, 'No Fire District'; three elected commissioners; property tax; only voters inside the boundary vote; the same ballot carries the commissioner races; majority in the statement vs three-fifths in RCW 52.02.110). It omits that the explanatory statement also names emergency medical services (S1), which is minor. cost_line matches S1, S2 and S9-S11. pro_summary includes a claim the dossier does not contain: 'is a tinderbox in summer'. The dossier quotes the statement as describing three evacuation notices since 2017, a three-day evacuation in 2020 with the fire contained 'eight' miles from the home by adjoining districts with state and federal support, and 'this section of the county has been overlooked for the formation of a fire district' (S1). No 'tinderbox' language appears. Unless the scorer has the pamphlet text, drop it. Suggested pro_summary: "The statement in favor (committee: Gerald Dotson, Christine Crisler and Truman Crisler) is a resident's account of three wildfire evacuation notices since 2017, including a three-day evacuation in 2020 while neighboring fire districts, with state and federal support, contained a wind-driven fire eight miles from his home. It says this part of the county has been overlooked for a fire district." con_summary matches S1.

Attacked on direction and strength: the 2027 amount ($50,000) is $10,000 below 2026's at a lower rate (S1, S4), so a yes vote might be read as a cut. It is not: the baseline for a no vote is no levy at all, which the district experienced in 2025 when the levy got 54.88% and failed (S4, S5, S7). A yes vote continues a recurring one-year tax, which maps to 1, like Wilson Creek and Spangle. A lower amount does not make it 0 or negative. S1 and S4 support the basis. No spending axis: the money pays for routine upkeep and restoring normal irrigation (S1, S4), which restores a prior level of service rather than expanding it.

what_it_does matches S1, S3 and S4 (seven cemeteries and one mausoleum; Waterville office; upkeep and irrigation; the 2025 levy fell short of 60% and the district cut irrigation, S4, S7; the 2026 levy passed at 64.33%, S6). cost_line matches S1 and S4 ($50,000 at about $0.22; 2026 was $60,000 at about $0.25), and $66 on $300,000 is correct arithmetic. pro_summary matches S1 (committee names; affordable cemetery services; rural cemetery upkeep; 'resume normal irrigation with upgraded systems'). con_summary matches S1.

missing.basis: A yes vote creates a public fire protection and emergency medical service, financed by a property tax levy, for an area that no fire district covers today.
missing.note: The dossier does not discuss spending. The measure is the clearest kind of public-investment expansion: it creates a new taxing government to provide fire protection and, per the explanatory statement, emergency medical services (S1) where county records show 'No Fire District' (S5, S6). The statement for frames it as filling a gap the county has 'overlooked' (S1). That matches the precedent of Shoreline's pool, mapped spending +1 for restoring a public service an area lacked. Strength 1, not 2, and medium confidence because no budget, staffing plan or levy rate is known (S1, S2), so the size of the expansion cannot be measured.
